title: Guru Har Rai's gurpurab

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Hargobind's gurpurab, and your line: two swords. Did you give a little courage and a little devotion where each was needed? Today, his grandson, who kept the swords and was remembered for flowers. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

There's a story Sikh children hear about a boy walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe. As he passes, the hem of the robe catches a flower and snaps its stem. The petals fall. His grandfather sees it and says something gentle: if you wear a robe like that, you have to carry it carefully. The boy is said to have held his robe gathered close for the rest of his life, so it would never break a flower again. That boy became the seventh Guru. Today: Guru Har Rai's gurpurab.
screen: `A ROBE CATCHES A FLOWER.` → `THE GRANDFATHER'S GENTLE WORD.` → `A ROBE HELD CLOSE FOR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Rai was born in 1630 at Kiratpur, in the foothills of the Himalayas, the grandson of Guru Hargobind. He became the seventh Guru in 1644, at about fourteen. The story of the flower is tradition, not a record, but it fits how Sikhs remember him: a gentle man, careful with living things. At Kiratpur, he's remembered for gardens: fruit trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs. Tradition says he kept a dispensary there, where medicines were made and given freely to anyone who came. He also kept the armed horsemen his grandfather had begun, but his years as Guru were largely peaceful. The best-known story about his medicine involves the Mughal court. Tradition tells that Dara Shikoh, the eldest son of the emperor Shah Jahan, fell gravely ill, and the court's physicians couldn't find a remedy. A rare herb was needed, and it was sent from Guru Har Rai's stores. Dara recovered. The striking part is who got the medicine: the son of the empire that had executed the Guru's great-grandfather, Guru Arjan. The healer didn't ask which side the patient was on. Sikh tradition sees in that the same teaching you've met all year: the One is in everyone, so care goes to everyone. His gurpurab is marked with kirtan and langar, and some gurdwaras and families mark it with things he'd recognize: planting trees, tending gardens, or volunteering in clinics. The healer, remembered by healing.
screen: `A GENTLE GURU AT KIRATPUR.` · `GARDENS AND A DISPENSARY.` · `MEDICINE FOR THE EMPEROR'S SON.` · `CARE FOR EVERYONE, NO SIDES.` · then, large: `THE HEALER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: water a plant. If there's a plant near you, bring it some water now, slowly, and watch the soil darken. If there isn't, picture one you love, or a tree you pass each day. As you water, think of one living thing you could be more careful with: a person, an animal, a place. Gather your robe, so to speak. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as the water goes in. The bell holds the time.
Guru Har Rai's gurpurab. The seventh Guru's birthday, remembered with gardens, herbs, and medicine given freely, even to the emperor's son.
Your line: the healer. Today, do one small act of care for something living, and do it without asking whose side it's on. Day six hundred eighty-eight.
